header_only_retrieval_assessment.scope: Local held-corpus comparison of generated search headings only, on two frozen browser work items and one genuine-advocate neighbouring control. No production edits, paid calls, new decomposition or ranking changes.
header_only_retrieval_assessment.conclusion: Generated Advocate passage headings measurably contaminate discovery and ranking. Removing them alone is not a satisfactory relevance fix: it removes observed advocate-topic noise for the drive dispute but loses useful deposit-dispute judgments at reranking and exposes other unrelated candidates. Do not claim overall retrieval acceptance from this experiment.

execution.latency_limit: Baseline ran first with cold model/index loading; paired elapsed time is not an unbiased speed comparison.
checks: Both frozen baseline arms reproduce all 24 saved browser root selections and their scores exactly.
All six arms completed lexical, semantic and rerank stages; existing ancestry/context gaps remain explicit partial search states.
Exact user-selected account words, legal enquiry texts, query IDs, corpus artifacts and current ranking behavior were preserved.
Production research/retrieval files and corpus manifests match their pre-run hashes.
Every recorded rerank window and winning score was independently reconstructed from current token-window logic without another inference.
execution.environment_note: The initial global-Python run could not load local dependencies. Its empty results are preserved but excluded. The measured run uses the browser's existing .venv-arrive interpreter.

findings.observation: On work w2, removing only the generated headings eliminates all three selected advocate-related provisions and four selected advocate-topic judgment roots. The four judgments vanish from the original-query discovery union, rather than merely moving below the final quota. Bar Council Rules paragraph 25 remains discovered but falls from rerank position 3 to 16; its score changes from 0.0169149 to 0.00168094.
findings.interpretation: The artificial provenance labels are functioning as legal-topic evidence. Provenance belongs in owned selections, not injected search words.

findings.observation: The w1 legal enquiries and their discovered useful sources are unchanged, but all formulations are flattened into one inquiry and split at 160 tokens. Removing headings shifts the second window from 'or bailment agreement...' to 'the hirer's remedies...'. All three useful sources remain in the rerank pool with unchanged enquiry discovery ranks; they then lose at the six-result selection.
findings.interpretation: This is a measured ranking-presentation loss, not failed discovery. The maximum of arbitrary fragment scores is sensitive to harmless header length. Useful bailment material previously won largely on the generic second window, not the complete qualified account. Simply retaining the polluted headers would preserve an accidental ranking benefit rather than fix the cause.

findings.observation: Both w1 arms still select six hire-purchase provisions although the account reports hire, not a purchase option. In the cleaned w2 arm, duplicate Sale of Goods Act section 47 roots and duplicate section 48 variants consume four provision slots, while Designs Act sections 12 and 14 consume the other two. The design passages govern restoration/registration and are unrelated to physical retention of the design drive. Cryogas paragraph 27_2 discusses copyright/design protection, not return of physical goods. In cleaned w1, Amlesh paragraph 18 concerns criminal-discovery evidence rather than an inspection report.
findings.interpretation: Topical similarity is still being mistaken for the relevant legal relationship. Removing the synthetic advocate word does not solve that broader problem; avoid replacing it with matter-specific exclusion terms or arbitrary score thresholds.

findings.observation: The neighbouring control retains the exact advocate/client account words. Cleaned results remain advocate-related, with the same Jamilabai, Pandurang and Ashwini roots retained; Supreme Court nonpayment/withdrawal Rule 17 moves from rank 4 to 1. This demonstrates that removing generated headings does not erase a genuinely supplied advocate role.
findings.limit: This is a narrow preservation control, not proof that the result answers the specific client-file retention issue. Several returned passages concern compromise authority or fees generally rather than retention of papers.

findings.observation: A read-only scan of the live indexed bare-act identity inventory (414710 passages) finds no Indian Contract Act identity. Identities containing 'contract' concern other enactments; identities containing '1872' return the Indian Evidence Act. The exact SQL and all identity matches are preserved in comparison-summary.json.
findings.limit: This establishes absence under the indexed Act identities searched, not absence from every upstream file or absence of a mislabelled source. It does not exclude judgments quoting Contract Act text.
findings.implication: A ranking change cannot recover a direct Contract Act passage that is not in the held index. Resolve corpus availability under its ingestion/identity owner separately from retrieval ranking.

recommended_next_atomic_step.first_measure: Keep the cleaned discovery pool frozen and rerank it against the complete exact selected original account alone, retaining exact source anchors and all account windows. This separates original-account focus from accidental concatenated legal-fragment influence.
recommended_next_atomic_step.why: It tests the focused-issue principle without changing decomposition, discovery, corpus, quotas or adding an API call. It may still fail; compare supported useful roots and unrelated admissions, not just score increases.
recommended_next_atomic_step.eventual_header_owner: If neutral query construction is promoted, version search-query construction/replay in research.py so old core_research_v4 saved queries continue to reconstruct exactly.
recommended_next_atomic_step.call_impact: No added API model call. The current experiment only replays local embedding/reranking.

account_only_rerank_assessment.decision: Do not promote original-account-only reranking. It fails the useful-source preservation requirement on the frozen deposit dispute and does not fix legal-relationship relevance on the drive dispute.
account_only_rerank_assessment.scope: Same three clean-header candidate pools from the earlier local comparison: two frozen browser disputes plus one genuine-advocate control. Only the reranker query was changed to the complete exact selected original account; no enquiry text was appended. All 698 source bodies and source anchors remained identical. Final root selection used the unchanged six-per-kind and two-per-judgment quotas.

execution.gpu_coordination: Started only after the other agent's 43-search run recorded state complete and GPU availability was confirmed.
verified: All six reranks completed without error.
Reconstructed source order and baseline quotas reproduce every previous clean-header selected root.
The production retrieval.py and frozen input evidence hashes remain unchanged.
Exact full account words, candidate bodies and anchors are preserved in the result evidence.
The full new window pairs and local model scores are preserved; no quality conclusion relies solely on model scores.

qualified_gains: Shaan Finance paragraph 9 returns from rank 14 to rank 1; its discussion of hire/bailment remains useful subject to its actual statutory context.
Amlesh paragraph 18, an unrelated criminal disclosure-evidence passage, falls from rank 4 to rank 131.
consequential_losses: Taj Mahal Hotel paragraph 16 falls from rank 9 to rank 131, rather than recovering the earlier browser selection. Its relevant bailment-care discussion is still absent from selected roots.
Rasiklal paragraph 58_7 falls from rank 20 to rank 143; the previously useful neighbouring section 171 discussion cannot be counted as returned by this root selection.

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam section 132 (professional communications) rises from rank 50 to rank 5 despite the dispute being about a hire deposit and damage. The account's ordinary client/document reporting is not a privilege dispute.

Raj Reddy Kallem paragraph 2 rises from rank 57 to rank 2. Its exact text recounts purchase, non-delivery, advance refund cheques and criminal proceedings concerning a laser cutting machine; those shared object words do not make it a passage about liability for damage after hired goods are returned.
Five of six selected provisions still concern hire-purchase, whose applicability is not established by the supplied hire account.
results.assessment: Mixed individual gains, clear failure to preserve important useful sources. General negligence and hire-purchase distinction passages may have analytical value, but do not compensate for the lost bailment-care and lien coverage.

results.case: w2: retention of original design drive
qualified_gains: Shipping Corporation paragraph 5_3 remains selected and moves from rank 4 to rank 2; it supplies a qualified contract-based retention analogy, not automatic applicability to this technician.

Sriyanesh Knitters paragraph 4_5 enters at rank 6. It distinguishes retention as security from sale powers and needs its statutory/professional limits preserved. This is useful conditional material; no new adjacent context was measured in this rerank-only pilot.
consequential_noise: Designs Act sections 14 and 12 are now the top two provisions. Their exact text concerns restoration and registration of designs, not a right to retain the physical drive.
Rasila S Mehta paragraph 13_21 becomes the top judgment. It concerns maintenance and repairs of attached flats and who pays the housing society, not bailment or retention of the supplied drive.
Dakshin Gujarat Vij paragraph 32 enters at rank 5. It concerns ownership/transfer of a captive generating plant and the meaning of set up, not the technician's limited setup purpose.

The remaining provisions include port and warehouse liens, electronic-record retention, and immovable-property lease obligations; their specific legal relationships cannot be silently transferred to the reported drive dispute.
results.assessment: Still confuses shared words with the legal relationship. Two useful judgment selections survive, but the returned set is not reliably relevant.

results.case: genuine advocate/client fee and file-retention control
qualified_gains: Fee-dispute taxation provisions now lead the provision results; these may be useful only within their actual court/proceeding scope.

B Sunitha paragraph 12 raises the burden of proving a disputed fee agreement, and Ashwini paragraph 45 addresses fees from client money held. These are relevant to the disputed-fees aspect, without establishing a lien over case papers.
The original advocate role and client interests remain represented; no genuine user word was removed.
results.remaining_gap: The control demonstrates role preservation and some useful fee material, not complete resolution of the right to retain case papers. Generic compromise/agency passages remain selected.
results.assessment: Some useful gains on this neighbour, insufficient to outweigh the failures on the two target disputes.

account_only_rerank_assessment.overall_interpretation: The original account is necessary for factual qualifications, but this local cross-encoder does not reliably recover the correct legal relationship from narrative alone. Conversely, blindly concatenating narrative and expansions lets arbitrary token-window tails dominate. Neither tested presentation should be treated as the completed relevance solution. No matter-specific filters, exclusions or score thresholds were added.
limitations: This is an exact-pool local reranking experiment, not an end-to-end browser acceptance run.
Previously observed corpus ancestry gaps and absence of an identifiable Indian Contract Act in the bare-act index remain unchanged.
New root context expansion was not run; a selected neighbouring root is not proof that all desired adjacent text was delivered.
No additional variants were run after this result.

historical_anchor_coverage.method: Reviewed exact owned Act identities and exact locators; reviewed Golden Set case identities and held original text readback. No substring title hit is counted. The raw lexical diagnostic remains separately preserved.
limits: Counts measure the historical named-anchor inventory, not precision, recall or legal applicability. Useful other sources are not marked wrong for lacking a named anchor.
Document presence, exact locator presence and connected provision readback are separate. A selected malformed or context-incomplete chunk is not promoted to validated law.
Historical Act editions, legal force, forum fit and current-law transitions remain unassessed. Name/ID matching is not E1 citation certification.
A read-pool omission cannot distinguish discovery failure from pre-read RRF pool loss for positions whose identity was never read. Per-position discovery traces are preserved.
Case anchors lack paragraph targets, so their counts mean expected judgment identity, not that the intended holding was retrieved.

65
For possession of immovable property or any interest therein based on title.
Twelve years
When the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff.
Explanation.-- For the purposes of this article --
(a) where the suit is by a remainderman, a reversioner (other than a landlord) or a devisee the possession of the defendant shall be deemed to become adverse only when the estate of the remainderman, reversioner or devisee, as the case may be, falls into possession;
(b) where the suit is by a Hindu or Muslim entitled to the possession of immovable property on the death of a Hindu or Muslim female, the possession of the defendant shall be deemed to become adverse only when the female dies;
(c) where the suit is by a purchaser at a sale in execution of a decree when the judgment-debtor was out of possession at the date of the sale, the purchaser shall be deemed to be a representative of the judgment-debtor who was out of possession.
STATE AMENDMENTS
1Bihar:
In Article 65, in the second column, following words shall be added at the end, namely:-- "but 30 years in respect of immovable property belonging to a member of the Schedule Tribes as specified in Part III to the Schedule to the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950".
2Orissa:
In Article 65, second column, following words shall be added at the end, namely:--
but thirty years in relation to immovable property belonging to a member of a Scheduled Tribe specified in respect of the State of Orissa in the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950.

138. Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account. —Where any cheque 
drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money 
to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt  or other 
liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of 
that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from 
that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an 
offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provision of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for 
4[a term which may be extended to two years’], or with fine which may extend to twic e the amount of the 
cheque, or with both: 
Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless— 
(a) thecheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on 
which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; 
(b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for 
the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice; in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, 
5[within thirty days] of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the 
cheque as unpaid; and 
(c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee 
or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of 
the said notice.

The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 — s.138: Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account. —Where any cheque
138. Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account. —Where any cheque 
drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money 
to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt  or other 
liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of 
that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from 
that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an 
offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provision of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for 
4[a term which may be extended to two years’], or with fine which may extend to twic e the amount of the 
cheque, or with both: 
Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless— 
(a) thecheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on 
which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; 
(b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for 
the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice; in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, 
5[within thirty days] of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the 
cheque as unpaid; and 
(c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee 
or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of 
the said notice. 
Explanation.—For the purposes of this section, “debt of other liability” means a legally enforceable debt 
or other liability.

cases.diagnosis: The operative section parent with occurrence suffix OCC2 is absent from the indexed passage DB but is retained under that exact owned key in bareacts_v3_parents.json. The raw statute retains its wording. Indexed proviso/clauses point to OCC2; the unrelated arrangement-of-sections heading is separately indexed as SECTION_138. Current resolution reads only indexed passages, so operative children fail while the 190-character heading can rank. This is an unintegrated parent-only source store plus repeated-occurrence distinction, not missing canonical law.

source_store_diagnosis.recommended_boundary: Model source lookup as indexed searchable passages plus owned contextual source records. Bind any parent-only store to a versioned corpus manifest/revision and durable exact-source identity before use. Preserve explicit distinctions among printed locator, occurrence, structural container and substantive parent. Do not insert contextual-only parents into vector positions or merge SECTION_138 with OCC2 by matching the printed number. Inspect source-store integration first; neither observation warrants a broad corpus rebuild.
limits: No current-law, legal applicability or completeness certification is made from these two examples.
The retained parent JSON currently lies outside the runtime manifest/revision; presence alone does not authorize silently treating it as trusted current context.
This diagnoses two causes only; other ambiguous roots may have different causes.
Parent-only context addition would need owned IDs and replay bindings; current position-based source identity cannot simply fabricate a vector position.
The separately measured account-only rerank experiment regressed; it is not recommended for promotion.
